item.title: When Helping Hurts
item.description:
Motivation

When Helping Hurts

How to recognize when your good intentions undermine someone else's growth.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Assessing readiness for change is key to better outcomes in healthcare.
  • The help we offer should match a person’s readiness to change.
  • Common signs can indicate that our helpful efforts are getting in the way of change.
Source: Pro-Stock Studio/Shutterstock

Can helping another person do more harm than good? That depends on how we define “help.” When we undermine another person’s autonomy, confidence, independence, freedom, growth, or power, we are not helping—we may be doing more harm than good. Real help implies doing what is best for another’s growth and development, not what is best for the person who wants to be helpful.

When we see someone facing a challenge or asking for help, the desire to help can be a natural impulse. But when someone asks for help, do they want to change? If you notice your child isn't following through on school responsibilities, what does it mean to help your child? Should we step in and help a co-worker behind on their work?

As you reflect on your own experiences helping others or being offered help, you already know helping isn't straightforward. Not everyone who asks for help is ready for change, and not everyone who appears to need help wants it. In healthcare, assessing readiness for change is key to improving outcomes. When our efforts to help don't match a person’s perception of their need for help or readiness for change, our help is not well received. This principle is similar in the home; we know that parental overinvolvement undermines students' academic success.

The Helper Role

There is a difference between helping and falling into the helper role. When we fall into the helper role, we are overly invested in the outcome of what we attempt to accomplish. We need people to follow our helpful advice to feel good about ourselves. When we are in the helper role rather than actually helping, we find purpose by getting others to change.

A key sign we are caught in the helper role is believing the person we are helping is powerless to help themselves. They need us to remind, motivate, and help them change.

How many times do we get hooked by that roommate or colleague who regularly leaves their empty food container on the counter, only two feet from the garbage can? If we feel compelled to help, we might first mention the container and nicely ask, “Are you done with that carry-out box on the counter?” The offending person knows we are not asking a question but making a complaint. But that is how the game progresses, and the person plays along. The response might be, “Oh yeah, thanks! I will get to it.” Several hours or days later, nothing changes. Then we get upset, throw out the box, and think we are helping by taking care of it ourselves.

We know that helping undermines growth when the person we are helping becomes dependent on us—they never learn to throw out their own garbage. The person being helped misses the opportunity to face challenges and solve problems on their own, undermining their autonomy, agency, and confidence.

The Yes-But Game

In healthcare, medical providers need to avoid falling into a predictable game that occurs when we dispense helpful advice about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and stress management.

Imagine a conversation between a physical therapist and a patient finishing up several weeks of therapy related to a motor vehicle accident. The patient asks, “What can I do to continue my progress when I am at home?” This seems like a straightforward request. Without checking the person’s readiness for change, the therapist, wanting to be helpful, suggests that the patient continue gentle rehabilitation exercises in a swimming pool.

This patient might not be ready for change, as we will see in their reply. The patient responds, “Yes, that is a good idea, but I don’t have money for an expensive fitness gym membership.” The therapist then reminds the patient they can easily use the nearby hotel pool for only $5 per use. Again, the patient responds, “Yes, but getting changed at the hotel into a swimsuit, showering, and getting dressed again takes too much time.” The classic yes-but game has begun, and the therapist would be better off changing tactics.

Not sensing a game being played, the therapist reminds the patient that if they start with simple exercises in the pool, they would eventually be able to use swimming as their strengthening and conditioning program. The therapist then emphasizes that an extended conditioning program will be necessary for full recovery for this patient—something that will require real commitment. The patient then says, “Yes, but if the water in the pool is not at least 74 degrees, then it will be too cold. Cold water flares up my pain. I can’t take that risk.” This response is like saying, “Checkmate!” in the yes-but game.

Signs We Are Not Helping

If you have found yourself getting hooked by the struggles of others, or offering help and advice to people who aren't receptive, here are five quick reminders your effort to help might be harmful:

  1. We remove choices by deciding for them.
  2. We remove risk and the need to face fears by doing it for them.
  3. We remove consequences for people's decisions by fixing the problems ourselves.
  4. We remove the reward of hard work and effort by offering an external reward rather than letting the person enjoy the internal reward of doing a good job.
  5. We remove the opportunity for growth by assuming a person is ready for change when we give advice.

Cultivating self-awareness in our interactions with others is important, especially when we are giving advice. If our goals for others and our desire to see them change do not match their ability to change, we may be setting a person up to see themselves as unable to change. I have talked with many patients with chronic pain who have been strongly encouraged by their medical doctor to start a running program to manage pain. As you might guess, not too many people are ready for that level of change and feel defeated by their inability to follow medical advice.

Start by asking questions about steps they have taken in the past to change, problems they have encountered with change, and a few small goals they believe they can reach now. This approach will not only better assess their readiness for change but also build a better connection with the person you are helping, which we know is a key ingredient of lasting change.

item.title: Reconciling With an Estranged Child: Listening Matters Most
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Reconciling With an Estranged Child: Listening Matters Most

Acknowledging another’s pain is not the same as accepting blame.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Focusing on understanding, not just being understood, can make all the difference in strained relationships.
  • Family estrangements are often prolonged when parents struggle with the need to defend their actions.
  • Parent and child may wish for reconciliation, but it can require humility that parents may find hard to offer.
  • Healing a relationship starts with accepting that our best intentions can have unforeseen negative impacts.

From my work with parents who have been estranged by their adult children, I’ve learned that few experiences match the pain that is felt when you’ve been cut off by someone you love. It may be difficult to believe, but parents are often taken by complete surprise when an adult child steps out of their life. Some children announce their intentions directly to their parents, but others are more subtle, and just stop responding to calls, texts, or emails. When the relationship breakdown resembles being “ghosted” by a child, parents tend to replay their most recent interactions repeatedly, trying to find a reason for the break.

However, when working with the adult children who decide to break away from their families-of-origin, their explanations tend to be very clear. They describe years of fraught relationships or share their frustration that their parents refused to understand the pain or distress they caused. Adult children often become exasperated when efforts to communicate their experiences or their needs to their parents are ignored or pushed aside. That can drive an adult child to simply walk away from the relationship. Parents may be persistent, at first, in their requests for explanations. But if their child's explanations are not received with the openness that the invitation seemed to imply, the estrangement grows more entrenched.

The Challenge of Multiple Realities

If a person is asked to think back to an event where others were present and asked to share their memory of the event, there’s a good chance that each person who was present is going to share a slightly, or markedly, different description of what happened. And each person is firmly going to believe that their memory of the event is accurate and valid. And for each person, it is their truth. People create their own realities from their own perspectives, and this leads to challenges in resolving family conflicts in which multiple realities compete.

Objective Perspectives Are Not Always Easy

When adult children recall having experienced the parent-child relationship differently than their parent does, it can be difficult for a parent to accept their child’s experience as a lived reality. They do not want to accept the possibility that their parenting strategies or relational behaviors may have been experienced as anything less than appropriate parenting. Parents, on the whole, make the best decisions they can. Unfortunately, sometimes the mistakes that they make arise from intentional efforts to “do the best that they can.” Parents may never have had a reason to consider any other perspective than their own – even when their adult child has made the decision to cut off contact.

“Please Understand My Side”

When a child cuts off their parents, the child carries the power in the relationship, and it their choice whether to attempt reconciliation or not. In many cases, what estranged adult children need most before considering reconnection is for their parent to understand the impact their behavior had on them. They need to be able to share their experiences without a parent rushing in to deny what the child knows as their truth.

Going on the Defensive Seldom Furthers Understanding

It’s helpful when parents recognize that intentions and impact are not the same thing. A parent’s best intentions do not erase the hurtful impact of their behavior. When an adult child shows up and expresses willingness to work through an impasse, they need their parents to acknowledge their experiences and their feelings. Unfortunately, parents may immediately move to a defensive position. Some may try to deny the reality that their child describes. Others leap to defend their choices and try to force their child to accept their own perspective. Common responses I’ve heard parents use include, “They’re remembering it wrong,” “They just won't understand why I did what I did,” or “I won’t take the blame for something that happened decades ago!” These types of responses do nothing to heal a ruptured relationship and are almost guaranteed to make the situation worse.

It can be undeniably unsettling to recognize that your actions have been experienced so differently from how you intended by people you love. That leads many parents to fear that if they validate their children’s feelings, they are accepting blame for the estrangement. When parents seek to defend their actions to, it leads them in a very different direction than if they seek to understand their child’s point of view. Accepting that multiple realities exist and that each person’s perspective is valid is a big step toward a new way of relating to your child.

Seeking to Understand Yourself Is a Good Place to Start

When parents seek support and guidance about the best response to their child’s request that they be willing to listen to, validate, and understand their side of the relationship, they often express hesitance or resistance. Some believe that if they are not allowed to defend themselves, they are admitting they are to blame. In these cases, it can be helpful for a parent to ask themselves questions like: What feelings do I experience when my child shares their concerns? What hurt might they most want me to acknowledge? And what does it mean if I acknowledge their pain?

Adult children do not want their concerns to be minimized or met with with explanations; they need their parents to accept that their own experiences are valid. Parents may need to focus less on being right about the past and more on understanding how their children were hurt.

Understanding Is a Beginning, but Not a Guarantee

While parents may deeply long for reconnection, this outcome is never guaranteed. An estranged child has the power to decide whether to work toward reconciliation or continue the estrangement. This underscores the importance of being willing to listen to your child’s side of the situation. If you refuse to listen, without rebuttal or denial, the chances for reconciliation drop dramatically. Accepting that your actions may have been received differently than you intended is not a sign of weakness or an admission of blame. It's an act of humility. For parents hoping to reconnect, when the focus becomes less about feeling understood and more about understanding their adult child’s perspective, true understanding can begin.

item.title: Abusers Hide Behind a Mask of Sanity
item.description:
Dark Tetrad

Abusers Hide Behind a Mask of Sanity

Techniques to see past the mask of the Dark Tetrad.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • The Dark Tetrad of narcissists, Machiavellians, psychopaths, and everyday Sadists are tricky to identify.
  • Research reveals the Dark Tetrad wear a mask of sanity which makes it challenging to identify them.
  • Learning how the Dark Tetrad are able to infiltrate workplaces provides strategies to recognize them.

Dr. Hervey Cleckley, a professor of psychiatry and neurology, wrote a seminal book The Mask of Sanity, which was published in 1941. It provided the first in-depth depiction of psychopathology, which is now integrated into the broader category of the Dark Tetrad: narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and everyday Sadism.

Cleckley’s insights are supported by advancements in psychology and neuroscience, but many are not trained to identify individuals who suffer from these traits. The key takeaway is the mask and learning to see past it can keep individuals and organizations safer. The Dark Tetrad wear a mask of healthy and positive mental traits, while beneath it resides a harmful self.

Our tendency is to think goodness and evil, kindness and cruelty, cannot subsist in the same individual. However, the Dark Tetrad are exemplars of this blend. Our tendency is to think that medicine effectively diagnoses Dark Tetrad disorders and enables the law to protects us from them. In fact, the Dark Tetrad are adept at sliding beneath the radar.

Cleckley tackles the significant problem facing medicine and law in that those who suffer from psychopathology appear sane, competent, and rational, even though they suffer from what he diagnoses as a “severe mental disorder” making them “more dangerous to themselves and to others” than mental patients who are institutionalized.

The Dark Tetrad wears a mask of positive psychological traits

In 2012, researchers Sun, Zhao, Yang and Fan show that positive psychological resources such as hope, efficacy, resilience, and optimism are not removed from those in the Dark Tetrad. Instead they blend in and fuel their aversive traits. The grandiosity of a narcissist, what Cleckley identifies as the trait of “pathological egocentricity,” makes them appear hopeful and optimistic.

The psychopath may appear calm and collected in crises and high-stress environments, but their resilience, as documented in the work of psychologists Babiak and Hare, and neuroscientist Baron-Cohen is grounded in a lack of emotions and empathy. Cleckley specifies psychopaths show “general poverty in major affective reactions,” and they specifically “lack remorse or shame.”

Cleckley notes that these individuals have an “absence of delusions and other signs of irrational thinking,” along with an “absence of nervousness” and “psychoneurotic manifestations.” Without identifiable markers of mental illness, it’s very difficult to assess the danger and harm of Dark Tetrad individuals.

Cleckley signals the “superficial charm” and “good intelligence” of psychopaths that further mislead us. Those with highly aversive traits—like those in the Dark Tetrad—will frequently have defenders, supporters, patrons, and even a cult-following. Despite this being well-established in history and research, we still struggle to avoid hiring and enabling disordered and dangerous individuals in workplaces.

The Dark Tetrad at work

Recent analysis of psychopaths confirm that they integrate as if mental stable and sane into the workforce and can be found concentrated in certain industries and roles. Professor Clive R. Boddy’s research found a greater concentration of psychopathic personalities in finance, insurance, government and education.

Even though these sectors require a great deal of trust, transparency, and fiduciary duty, they are not adept at ensuring those prone to dishonesty, manipulation, and deception are kept at bay. Boddy found that approximately 28% of participants in the study reported “psychopathic behaviour” in governmental and educational settings.

Forensic psychologist, author of Working with Monsters, Dr. John Clarke notes that psychopathic personalities are attracted to power, prestige, and risk-taking. They seek industries with power structures (government and education), along with those offering monetary gain and risk (finance and insurance).

Strategies to see beyond the Dark Tetrad’s mask

Source: Campaign Creators / Pixabay

In The Gaslit Brain, Dr. Jennifer Fraser designed a multi-pronged strategy to better identify the Dark Tetrad at work. Each of the proven ways to see through the fictional mask of the abuser is informed by neuroscientific research.

Step 1: Gaslighting – defined by Merriam-Webster dictionary in 2022 as the “act or practice of grossly misleading someone, especially for personal advantage"—is one of the Dark Tetrad’s favourite weapons. Step one in identifying gaslighting’s harmful effects is to keep your brain healthy and fit. Your neuroplasticity – your brain’s ability to strengthen based on deliberate practice—means you can practice skepticism, practice asking questions rather than simply believing, practice focusing on acts rather than words, track record rather than promises.

Step 2: The Dark Tetrad strive to interrupt and confuse your relationship with your own inner-self. It not only makes you doubt your mind’s ability to assess reality or sort through memories, it also tries to make you misinterpret or dismiss the wealth of information you get from your instinctual systems. Pay attention to temperature, heart rate, gut distress, tension in muscles, bracing of your body. Your gut instinct is highly adept at giving you important information that can keep you safer. The goal is to develop accurate and nuanced vocabulary to interpret what it’s telling your brain.

Step 3: Manipulators who wear the mask of trustworthiness, reliability, optimism and resilience, who capitalize on their charisma and intelligence, often use your fear of shame or even disappointment that could lead you to be blocked from your community, as a way to distract you with fear. When your brain focuses on threat, it struggles to problem-solve, be productive or creative that the abuser uses to confirm their discrediting of you in the community. Learn to identify rising stress and instead of withdrawing, lean in to connections. Resist the impulse to isolate, and instead prioritize relationships. Mindfulness, exercise, being in nature are all well-backed by research to lower stress levels and return agency to you. In that more calm state, strategize.

Finally, the Dark Tetrad has no problem telling self-serving lies or using their power, prestige, and social credibility to hide the destructive person behind the mask. Their goal is to make you complicit: do not dismiss micro-aggressions or early signs of concerning conduct; do not default to doubting those who report the abuser; do not give second chances or you run the risk of being complicit with the harm they do.

item.title: When Someone You Love Dies, Who Do You Become?
item.description:
Grief

When Someone You Love Dies, Who Do You Become?

Losing someone we love can also mean losing the person we were together.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Grief can involve losing a shared future and questioning who we are without the person who died.
  • Adapting to loss can mean moving between mourning and attending to the demands of a changed life.
  • The relationships that shaped us remain part of who we become through memories, values, and everyday actions.
Vision sits in a theater
Source: Marvel Studios

When someone we love dies, we can feel like we’ve lost the person we share our good news with, the person who knows our true selves, or the person who remembers earlier versions of ourselves and our relationships. We may wonder what our future will be without them.

We don’t just grieve the loss of the person; we grieve the future we won’t be spending with them. Underneath these feelings is another concern, though, and one that may be harder to name: We may wonder who we are without that person.

Marvel’s new series, VisionQuest, gives this question an unusual form. Its central character is a synthezoid trying to understand his memories, his relationships, and himself. Beneath the vibranium is a recognizable human experience: the struggle to make sense of a life that no longer feels like our own. (Note: There are spoilers ahead.)

Remembering a Life That Feels Far Away

In VisionQuest, a rebuilt Vision carries memories of his relationship with Wanda Maximoff, but he consistently clarifies that he is not the old Vision, the “real” Vision. This rebuilt Vision’s search for meaning becomes a search for identity. Given the complexities of the technology that created and rebuilt Vision, viewers may be likely to believe that this version is not the “real” Vision. Read through the lens of grief, however, there is another possibility.

When we grieve, we may question how the life we remember with our loved one feels so far away. We may remember our old selves while struggling to reconnect with how we felt then. A video may show us laughing with the person we loved and have since lost. We remember the occasion, the conversation, perhaps even what happened just after the video was recorded, but we may struggle to recognize the person we were then. That person lived in a world where a particular future still seemed possible.

Vision’s experience offers viewers a way to understand this experience. Having access to the past does not automatically tell us how to live in the present.

We Grieve Who We Were Together

In the finale of VisionQuest, Ultron states that “grief isn’t love, it’s fear.” Vision confirms that he believes the same, but adds that it’s “fear that without them, you’re no one. Inconsequential. An untethered thing that can all too easily float away and disappear. Alone.” This exchange asks Ultron, Vision, and viewers to confront the fear that losing someone we love also means losing part of who we are.

As a family scientist, I am drawn to the relational question at the center of this story. Our identities develop within relationships. We become someone’s partner, parent, child, sibling, or closest friend. Over time, those relationships help organize our routines, responsibilities, and expectations. When someone dies, we may lose a person who knew how to comfort us, challenge us, or make us laugh. We may also lose everyday opportunities to be a particular version of ourselves. Grief can unsettle our identities. We may ask who we are when we no longer care for our parents each afternoon, what it means to be a spouse when our partners are gone, or where we put the affection that once had a destination.

Research on meaning reconstruction examines how people make sense of loss and rebuild their identities afterward. One study of bereaved young adults found that positive identity change was associated with fewer grief complications. This does not mean people must find a benefit in someone’s death. It suggests that understanding who we are becoming can matter alongside understanding what we have lost.

Grief Leaves Room for Ordinary Life

A story about an android or synthezoid might tempt us to imagine grief as a problem that could be fixed, if only we had enough information or faster processing speeds. If we could understand everything, perhaps we could stop hurting, but understanding a death and adapting to its consequences are different tasks.

Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut’s dual process model describes movement between attending to loss and attending to the demands of a changed life. We might spend an evening immersed in memories, then spend the next morning learning to manage a responsibility our loved one once handled. Taking a break from grief is part of the model, too.

That perspective makes room for experiences that can otherwise feel contradictory. We can miss someone and enjoy dinner with friends. We can feel capable one day and overwhelmed the next. For viewers, Vision’s search offers a useful perspective on what it means to participate in life, like creating a relationship with his son, while carrying an unfinished relationship with the past.

We may find ways to carry that relationship into our present lives through small, everyday actions. We repeat a loved one’s joke or favorite phrase. We teach a child something our loved one taught us. We make a decision informed by their kindness—or decide to live differently from them. We may never become the person we were before the loss, but the relationships that helped shape us can remain part of who we become.

Marvel vs. Psychology

Marvel says: Grief can be frightening because losing someone we love can leave us questioning who we are without them. Vision gives voice to the fear that we might become untethered without the relationships that helped define us.

Psychology says: Fear can be part of grief. Losing someone can unsettle our identity, but adapting to the new identity does not require erasing the relationship. We can move between mourning what we have lost and building a changed life. We can carry parts of that relationship into who we become.

The Verdict: For a story about synthezoids, Marvel’s portrayal of grief feels deeply human. I’m still reflecting on this episode and series, and on how my own experiences with grief have shaped who I am.

item.title: The 4 Ways People Process Mind-Altering Experiences
item.description:
Spirituality

The 4 Ways People Process Mind-Altering Experiences

Why some transform quickly after an exceptional experience while others struggle.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Psychedelic, near-death, and other exceptional experiences can transform, but integration takes time.
  • Research suggests people follow one of four pathways, ranging from swift acceptance to prolonged struggle.
  • Discerning support and gradual reflection help; rushing back or chasing the high can keep people stuck.

Co-authored by Mark Shelvock and Joelle Adams

Source: Lianhao Qu/Unsplash

It’s an ordinary Monday; you’re buttering toast, answering emails, and negotiating with the dog about when it’s time to go for a walk. Underneath all of it, a question keeps surfacing in your psyche: What happened to me?

Maybe three weeks ago, on a psilocybin retreat, you dissolved into the universe and haven’t entirely come back. Perhaps during surgery, you watched the medical team from somewhere near the ceiling and had a near-death experience. When you finally tell someone, their reaction in those first few seconds may shape how you carry this for years.

If this sounds familiar, you’re in larger company than you might think. Meditation teacher Jack Kornfield named this predicament decades ago; after the ecstasy comes the laundry.1 The experience is over, and the work of figuring out what to do with it has just begun.

The good news is that people have been mapping this terrain for a long time.

Maps for return

Spiritual teachers have identified various pathways that experiencers take following psychedelic and other events such as near-death, out-of-body, spontaneous spiritual awakening, kundalini, alien or UFO, and similar exceptional experiences that alter consciousness and challenge concepts of reality.

Carl Jung, who described his own near-death experience after a heart attack in 1944, saw such moments as encounters with the deeper layers of the psyche.2 In his view, what surfaces in these states, including the shadow and archetypal images shared across cultures, needs to be gradually integrated into conscious life. He called this lifelong process individuation, which means becoming more fully and authentically oneself.

Rhea White and Suzanne Brown mapped five stages experiencers tend to move through following exceptional experiences.3 First, the initiating event itself, during which the experiencers’ ordinary worlds are disrupted by an experience that leaves them questioning the nature of reality. Then the search for reconciliation, during which experiencers try to make sense of what happened to them by seeking out others who have had similar experiences and looking for frameworks that explain the event. In the between two worlds stage, people begin bringing their new understanding of reality into daily life but often feel pulled in two directions: unable to fully embrace this new reality, yet unable to return to the beliefs they held before.

In the experiential paradigm, as the experiencer moves to the next stage, they begin to accept what happened during the initiating event and fully integrate their new perspectives into their daily lives. Finally, the experiencer finds a new way of being in the world, characterized by alignment to one’s purpose and a desire to be of service. Once a psycho-spiritually transformative experience has been woven into this new way of living, White and Brown call it an "exceptional human experience." Rather than a ladder to climb, these stages are more like landmarks on a winding path; people may begin anywhere, double back, or revisit a stage more than once.

New pathway models

Early findings from a recent preprint study point to more nuanced pathways people may take after a psychedelic or other exceptional experience. One of us (Joelle Adams), along with colleagues Pascal Michael and David Luke, found that experiencers tend to follow one of four pathways: challenging, what goes up, slow flow, or deep surrender.4

On the challenging pathway, people struggle to make sense of what happened and may experience depersonalization, derealization, depression and anxiety, sleep disturbances, and other symptoms that undermine their well-being. Those on the what goes up pathway report an initial "high" following their experience, a period of positive mood, energy, clarity, and alignment with the universe. This is followed by a longer "low" when they face psychological, physical, relational, and spiritual challenges. They may chase the initial high, seeking repeat experiences to recapture those early feelings. Eventually, with professional support and meaningful changes in their lives, they can find a new equilibrium, much like White and Brown’s new way of being in the world stage.

Adams, Michael, and Luke also found that some experiencers follow an iterative pathway: the slow flow. Following the initial experience, they take their time to process what happened and integrate new perspectives and insights into their lives, coming to a place of equilibrium. Only then do they seek out or initiate new events or altered states of consciousness. Finally, those on the deep surrender pathway report integrating their experiences with relative ease, accepting and surrendering to new insights and concepts of reality. They often change their life circumstances, such as jobs and relationships, quite quickly, and report few challenges in returning to homeostasis.

Help along the path

For those who find an experience difficult to integrate, the company of others who have walked this path can be invaluable. Sharing the experience with a trusted friend, or with a therapist who is open to non-ordinary states and approaches them without pathologizing, can provide the steadiness needed to make meaning of a reality-altering event. Reading, podcasts, and workshops can offer both frameworks for understanding and the quiet reassurance that others have travelled similar terrain, though some people find this material overwhelming and benefit from taking it in gradually. Solitude, time in nature, journaling, and creative expression are also frequently described as essential companions to integration.

Discernment matters too. Confiding in someone who dismisses or misunderstands the experience can deepen the isolation it so often brings. Likewise, rushing back into the demands of daily life without pausing to reflect can leave the experience unprocessed and, at times, psychologically destabilizing. Chasing a return to the original high, or clinging rigidly to any single framework for explaining what happened, can also keep people stuck. Meditation and other spiritual practices can sometimes aid integration, though for some they may reactivate difficult emotional states; it’s often wise to proceed gradually and with compassionate support.

Source: Jamie Street/Unsplash

In the end, integration doesn't fully happen on the idealized spiritual mountaintop. More commonly, people learn to let their insights shape how they live, work, and love, becoming, in Jung’s sense, more fully themselves. With support, time, patience, and conscious intentionality, these experiences can lead to greater well-being, deeper empathy, and a quieter fear of death. The toast still needs buttering and the dog still needs walking, but the difference is who is doing it.

This post was co-authored by Mark Shelvock and Joelle Adams. Joelle is a researcher, writer, and teacher with an interest in the psychological effects of psychedelic and other exceptional experiences.
